XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 5. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Contaminated land
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
The recent BBC documentary Buried, presented by Michael Sheen, has brought renewed attention to this issue of contaminated land, which I very much welcome, and I would like to thank all of those who have been involved in its production. However, we must recognise that, for many communities, these concerns have been raised by them for many years. Campaigners and communities across Wales have been raising these issues with us, and quite a few of them are actually up there in the gallery today.

And I've seen the impact of that legacy first-hand in my own constituency. In Ynysddu, Ty Llwyd quarry was actually featured in the recent documentary, with the two Jans. It's a site where local people have been raising concerns for years about the historical disposal of chemical waste, its links to Monsanto's former manufacturing plant in Newport and what that legacy could mean for the surrounding community. There have also been concerns about leachate leaving the former quarry site, particularly following periods of heavy rainfall, and the potential for contaminants to move then into the surrounding area.

I want to take this opportunity to thank Councillor Janine Reid, who is here as well today, and also her colleague Councillor Jan Jones, for the tireless work that they have done to raise these concerns and make sure that their community's voice is heard.

But, ultimately, Ty Llwyd is about more than what is happening at a former quarry site. It's about the people who live alongside it. For those people, this is not an abstract environmental issue. It's something that's been hanging over the community for years. It's about the place where people live, where their children have grown up and where people go and walk their dogs. It's about being able to feel confident that the place they call home is safe and that their community and its future are being protected.

As Councillor Reid put it:

'For our community, Ty Llwyd is not an abstract environmental issue—it is something that has been hanging over us for years. The consequences of what has happened here are felt by the people who live alongside it.

'We need the contamination to be properly understood, the risks to our community to be taken seriously, and a clear plan to ensure that Ty Llwyd along with other sites in Wales, do not continue to be a source of concern for local people—with reassurance that our community and its future are being protected.'

And I think that quote from Janine gets to the real heart of this issue today. People shouldn't have to live for years with unanswered questions about what may be beneath their feet, what may be moving through the land around them, or what the potential risks could be. They deserve clear information about what is known, a proper understanding of the risks, and confidence that there is a clear plan in place on how we deal with those risks. And, as we know, Ty Llwyd is not unique. Across Wales, there are thousands of sites with a history of industrial or other potentially contaminating activity—from north to south, from Cefn Mawr to Maendy, communities across Wales are living alongside that legacy.

Research by Friends of the Earth Cymru has identified more than 45,000 potentially contaminated land sites across Wales. And while that gives us some indication of the scale of this issue, it also highlights the fact that we still do not have a clear national picture of potentially contaminated land across Wales. We need to know where these sites are, what contaminants may be present and which pose the greatest risks to our communities and to our environment. And that is why this motion today calls for a national framework for the testing and assessment of potentially contaminated land, prioritising those sites that pose the greatest risks. We need to know where these sites are. We need to understand what contamination may be present and the risks it poses. And we need to make sure that the sites presenting the greatest risks are prioritised.

But there is also another important issue here, and that is who pays. The principle of 'polluters pay' should be at the heart of this approach. Where the person or the company responsible for pollution can be identified and held responsible, they should contribute towards the costs of putting it right. That burden should not simply fall on our local authorities, and it shouldn't fall on the taxpayers either.

But. of course, as we know, with historical contamination it's not always straightforward. Some companies may no longer exist. Ownership may have changed. Records may be incomplete. That's why the motion also calls for the UK Government to introduce a dedicated funding mechanism for cases where the costs cannot be recovered, because there has to be a solution for those sites as well. We cannot have a situation where a local authority knows there is a potential problem, but does not have the resources to properly address it. And we cannot expect communities to carry the burden of historical industrial activity simply because the pollution happened many years ago.

Local authorities, Natural Resources Wales and other organisations are already doing important work in identifying, investigating and managing contaminated land. But they need the resources and the support to fulfil those responsibilities. And communities need confidence that, when they raise concerns, those concerns will be properly investigated.

So, Dirprwy Lywydd, this motion is ultimately about making sure that the legacy of our industrial past is managed properly and fairly. It's about having a clearer national picture of contaminated land. It's about prioritising the sites where the risks are greatest. It's about giving local authorities the support that they need. And it's about making sure that, where possible, those responsible for pollution contribute to the cost of putting it right.

The communities living alongside these sites did not create this contamination, so they should not be left with carrying the uncertainty, the potential risks or the costs. For those reasons, Dirprwy Lywydd, I hope Members across the Siambr will support this motion today. Diolch yn fawr.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Mae rhaglen ddogfen ddiweddar ar y BBC, Buried, a gyflwynwyd gan Michael Sheen, wedi tynnu sylw o'r newydd at broblem tir halogedig, ac rwy'n croesawu hynny'n fawr, a hoffwn ddiolch i bawb a gymerodd ran yn y gwaith o'i chynhyrchu. Fodd bynnag, rhaid inni gydnabod, i lawer o gymunedau, fod y pryderon hyn wedi cael eu codi ganddynt ers blynyddoedd lawer. Mae ymgyrchwyr a chymunedau ledled Cymru wedi bod yn codi'r materion hyn gyda ni, ac mae cryn dipyn ohonynt i fyny yn yr oriel heddiw mewn gwirionedd.

Ac rwyf wedi gweld effaith y gwaddol hwnnw yn fy etholaeth i. Yn Ynys-ddu, roedd sylw i chwarel Tŷ Llwyd ar y rhaglen ddogfen, gyda'r ddwy Jan. Mae'n safle lle mae pobl leol wedi bod yn codi pryderon ers blynyddoedd ynghylch gwastraff cemegol a waredwyd yn hanesyddol, ei gysylltiadau â hen ffatri weithgynhyrchu Monsanto yng Nghasnewydd a'r hyn y gallai'r gwaddol hwnnw ei olygu i'r gymuned gyfagos. Mynegwyd pryderon hefyd ynghylch trwytholch yn gadael safle'r hen chwarel, yn enwedig yn sgil cyfnodau o law trwm, a'r perygl i halogion symud wedyn i mewn i'r ardal gyfagos.

Hoffwn achub ar y cyfle hwn i ddiolch i'r Cynghorydd Janine Reid, sydd yma heddiw hefyd, ac i'w chydweithiwr y Cynghorydd Jan Jones, am y gwaith diflino y maent wedi'i wneud i godi'r pryderon hyn a sicrhau bod llais eu cymuned yn cael ei glywed.

Ond yn y pen draw, mae a wnelo Tŷ Llwyd â mwy na'r hyn sy'n digwydd mewn hen safle chwarel. Mae a wnelo â'r bobl sy'n byw wrth ei ymyl. I'r bobl hynny, nid mater amgylcheddol haniaethol yw hwn. Mae'n rhywbeth sydd wedi bod yn hongian dros y gymuned ers blynyddoedd. Mae a wnelo â'r fan lle mae pobl yn byw, lle mae eu plant wedi tyfu i fyny a lle mae pobl yn mynd i gerdded eu cŵn. Mae a wnelo â gallu teimlo'n hyderus fod y lle maent yn ei alw'n gartref yn ddiogel a bod eu cymuned a'i dyfodol yn cael eu diogelu.

Fel y dywedodd y Cynghorydd Reid:

'I’n cymuned ni, nid mater amgylcheddol yn unig yw Tŷ Llwyd, mae’n rhywbeth sydd wedi bod yn hongian drosom ers blynyddoedd. Mae canlyniadau’r hyn sydd wedi digwydd yma yn cael eu teimlo gan y bobl sy’n byw ochr yn ochr ag ef.'

Mae angen inni ddeall yr halogiad yn iawn, mae angen i'r peryglon i'n cymuned gael eu cymryd o ddifrif, ac mae angen cynllun clir i sicrhau nad yw Tŷ Llwyd, ynghyd â safleoedd eraill yng Nghymru, yn parhau i fod yn destun pryder i bobl leol—gyda sicrwydd fod ein cymuned a'i dyfodol yn cael eu diogelu.

A chredaf fod y dyfyniad hwnnw gan Janine yn mynd at wraidd y mater hwn heddiw. Ni ddylai pobl orfod byw am flynyddoedd gyda chwestiynau heb eu hateb ynglŷn â’r hyn a allai fod o dan eu traed, yr hyn a allai fod yn symud drwy'r tir o'u cwmpas, neu beth y gallai'r peryglon posibl fod. Maent yn haeddu gwybodaeth glir ynglŷn â’r hyn sy'n hysbys, dealltwriaeth briodol o'r peryglon, a hyder fod cynllun clir ar waith o ran sut yr awn ati i ddelio â'r peryglon hynny. Ac fel y gwyddom, nid yw Tŷ Llwyd yn unigryw. Ledled Cymru, mae yna filoedd o safleoedd sydd â hanes o weithgarwch diwydiannol neu weithgarwch arall a allai achosi halogiad—o'r gogledd i'r de, o Gefn-mawr i'r Maendy, mae cymunedau ledled Cymru yn byw ochr yn ochr â'r gwaddol hwnnw.

Mae ymchwil gan Cyfeillion y Ddaear Cymru wedi nodi mwy na 45,000 o safleoedd tir halogedig posibl ledled Cymru. Ac er bod hynny'n rhoi rhywfaint o syniad i ni o faint y broblem hon, mae hefyd yn tynnu sylw at y ffaith nad oes gennym ddarlun cenedlaethol clir o hyd o dir halogedig posibl ledled Cymru. Mae angen inni wybod ble mae'r safleoedd hyn, pa halogion a allai fod yn bresennol a pha rai sy'n achosi'r risg fwyaf i'n cymunedau ac i'n hamgylchedd. A dyna pam y mae'r cynnig hwn heddiw yn galw am fframwaith cenedlaethol ar gyfer profi ac asesu tir halogedig posibl, gan flaenoriaethu'r safleoedd sy'n achosi'r risg fwyaf. Mae angen inni wybod ble mae'r safleoedd hyn. Mae angen inni ddeall pa halogiad a allai fod yn bresennol a'r risg y mae'n eu hachosi. Ac mae angen inni sicrhau bod y safleoedd sy'n achosi'r risg fwyaf yn cael eu blaenoriaethu.

Ond mae mater pwysig arall yma hefyd, sef pwy sy'n talu. Dylai'r egwyddor mai’r llygrwr sy’n talu fod wrth wraidd y dull hwn o weithredu. Lle gellir nodi pwy yw'r unigolyn neu'r cwmni sy'n gyfrifol am lygru a'u dwyn i gyfrif, dylent gyfrannu at gostau unioni'r sefyllfa. Ni ddylai'r baich hwnnw ddisgyn ar ein hawdurdodau lleol yn unig, ac ni ddylai ddisgyn ar y trethdalwyr chwaith.

Ond wrth gwrs, fel y gwyddom, gyda halogiad hanesyddol, nid yw bob amser yn syml. Efallai fod rhai cwmnïau nad ydynt yn bodoli mwyach. Efallai fod perchnogaeth wedi newid. Efallai fod cofnodion yn anghyflawn. Dyna pam y mae'r cynnig hefyd yn galw ar Lywodraeth y DU i gyflwyno mecanwaith ariannu pwrpasol ar gyfer achosion lle na ellir adennill y costau, gan fod yn rhaid bod ateb ar gyfer y safleoedd hynny hefyd. Ni allwn gael sefyllfa lle mae awdurdod lleol yn gwybod bod problem bosibl, ond nad oes ganddo'r adnoddau i fynd i'r afael â hi'n iawn. Ac ni allwn ddisgwyl i gymunedau ysgwyddo baich gweithgarwch diwydiannol hanesyddol am fod y llygru wedi digwydd flynyddoedd lawer yn ôl.

Mae awdurdodau lleol, Cyfoeth Naturiol Cymru a sefydliadau eraill eisoes yn gwneud gwaith pwysig yn nodi, ymchwilio a rheoli tir halogedig. Ond mae angen adnoddau a chymorth arnynt i gyflawni'r cyfrifoldebau hynny. Ac mae angen hyder ar gymunedau, pan fyddant yn codi pryderon, y bydd y pryderon hynny'n cael eu harchwilio'n briodol.

Felly, Ddirprwy Lywydd, yn y pen draw, mae a wnelo'r cynnig hwn â sicrhau bod gwaddol ein gorffennol diwydiannol yn cael ei reoli'n briodol ac yn deg. Mae a wnelo â chael darlun cenedlaethol cliriach o dir halogedig. Mae a wnelo â blaenoriaethu'r safleoedd lle mae'r peryglon mwyaf yn bodoli. Mae a wnelo â darparu'r cymorth sydd ei angen ar awdurdodau lleol. Ac mae a wnelo â sicrhau, lle bo modd, fod y rhai sy'n gyfrifol am lygredd yn cyfrannu at gost ei unioni.

Nid y cymunedau sy'n byw ochr yn ochr â'r safleoedd hyn a greodd yr halogiad hwn, felly ni ddylent orfod ysgwyddo'r ansicrwydd, y peryglon posibl na'r costau. Am y rhesymau hynny, Ddirprwy Lywydd, rwy'n gobeithio y bydd Aelodau ar draws y Siambr yn cefnogi'r cynnig hwn heddiw. Diolch yn fawr.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Thank you for bringing this motion together today. From Agent Orange production to genetically modified organism controversies, Monsanto has been at the heart of it. This agricultural giant's legacy includes toxic chemicals, patent disputes and environmental damage, leading to lawsuits and ongoing health concerns worldwide.

Monsanto's controversial legacy has left an indelible mark on agricultural global health and the environment. The agrochemical giant's decades-long history includes production of toxic chemicals like Agent Orange, PCBs, polychlorinated biphenyls, and DDT, dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane, while its aggressive patenting of genetically modified seeds has sparked intense debate about food sovereignty and farmers’ rights. From lawsuits over cancer-causing pesticides to allegations of suppressing scientific research, you'll discover why Monsanto has become one of the most criticised corporations in modern history. Many critics argue that Monsanto's business practices prioritise profits over public health and environmental safety, leading to lasting consequences we're still grappling with today.

Monsanto began in 1901 as a chemical manufacturer producing saccharin. By the 1940s they expanded into agricultural chemicals, including DDT and Agent Orange. The company shifted focus to biotechnology in the 1980s, launching the first genetically modified crops in 1996 through their flagship product, Roundup Ready soya beans. Monsanto's production of PCBs led to widespread environmental contamination, with devastating effects on local communities. Monsanto operated a PCB manufacturing plant in Anniston, USA from 1929 to 1971, dumping toxic waste into local waterways. The contamination left residents with high rates of cancer, liver disease and diabetes, while polluting the soil and water systems. Testing revealed PCB levels 200 times higher than the federal safety limit in local creeks. Internal documents reveal that Monsanto knew about PCB dangers as early as 1937, but continued production until 1977. The company buried contaminated soil in unlined landfills. In 2003, Monsanto paid $700 million to settle claims by 20,000 Anniston residents over PCB contamination. Monsanto's decades-long history of corporate misconduct has left an indelible mark on public health, environmental safety and agricultural independence. From the devastating effects of Agent Orange to the ongoing Roundup controversy, their actions continue to impact millions of lives worldwide.

Their acquisition by Bayer—something I'm sure they regret—hasn't eased the company's troubled legacy, as lawsuits and health concerns persist. You'll find that the Monsanto story serves as a stark reminder of how corporate profits often overshadow public welfare. In 1919, the US chemical company Monsanto entered into partnership with Graesser's chemical works at Cefn Mawr to produce vanillin, salicylic acid, aspirin, and, later, rubber-processing chemicals. The site was later operated by Flexsys, a subsidiary of Solutia, but production ceased in 2010.

The alleged dumping of PCBs, poisonous chemicals that do not break down but build up in the environment, animals, fish and humans over time, are widespread. These chemicals were dumped in 12 known sites across Wales, including in Rhiwabon, Cefn Mawr and the infamous Llwyneinion acid tar lagoon near Rhosllanerchrugog. Evidence gathered by campaigners and experts over years claims that PCBs may have been responsible for spikes in rare cancers in those areas. A local resident, featured in Buried with Michael Sheen, Michael Phillips, revealed that, as children, he and his friends went down to Llwyneinion acid lagoon to watch as fire crews battled to bring a fire there under control in 1980. The fire took 18 hours to extinguish, but, years later, Michael and his friends all contracted rare cancers, which he attributes to exposure to PCBs. And he says, 'My surgeon said, "This is strange, I've never seen this type of cancer before" and he'd had this distinguished career of 40 years', said Phillips. Two of his friends have passed away, with brain cancer and breast cancer. Another is battling brain cancer, while a fourth had all his lymph nodes removed, as they were cancerous. A fifth even had the same type of cancer as Phillips—something his surgeon said was equivalent to the odds of winning the lottery every day for six months.

And that's the reality today of the situation left behind by the worst of multinational capitalism. At the end of the day, it's about people, about their and our environment. It's about the potential threats to them, their families, children and future generations. And that's why we owe it to them to demand action and put a strategic framework and plan of action in place. Diolch yn fawr.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Diolch am ddod â'r cynnig hwn at ei gilydd heddiw. O gynhyrchiant Agent Orange i ddadleuon ynghylch organebau a addaswyd yn enetig, mae Monsanto wedi bod wrth wraidd y cyfan. Mae gwaddol y cawr amaethyddol hwn yn cynnwys cemegau gwenwynig, anghydfodau ynghylch patentau a niwed amgylcheddol, gan arwain at achosion cyfreithiol a phryderon iechyd parhaus ledled y byd.

Mae gwaddol dadleuol Monsanto wedi gadael marc parhaol ar iechyd amaethyddol byd-eang a'r amgylchedd. Mae hanes hirfaith y cawr agrocemegol hwn yn cynnwys cynhyrchu cemegau gwenwynig fel Agent Orange, PCBs, biffenylau polyclorinedig, a DDT, deuglorodeuffenyltricloroethan, tra bo'i ymgyrch ddiflino i batentu hadau a addaswyd yn enetig wedi sbarduno dadlau dwys ynghylch sofraniaeth bwyd a hawliau ffermwyr. O achosion cyfreithiol ynghylch plaladdwyr sy'n achosi canser i honiadau o atal ymchwil wyddonol, fe welwch pam y mae Monsanto wedi dod yn un o'r corfforaethau a gafodd eu beirniadu fwyaf yn y cyfnod modern. Mae llawer o feirniaid yn dadlau bod arferion busnes Monsanto yn blaenoriaethu elw dros iechyd y cyhoedd a diogelwch amgylcheddol, gan arwain at ganlyniadau parhaol rydym yn dal i ymrafael â nhw heddiw.

Sefydlwyd Monsanto ym 1901 fel gwneuthurwr cemegau a gynhyrchai sacarin. Erbyn y 1940au, roeddent wedi ehangu i faes cemegau amaethyddol, gan gynnwys DDT ac Agent Orange. Newidiodd y cwmni ei ffocws i fiotechnoleg yn y 1980au, gan lansio'r cnydau cyntaf a addaswyd yn enetig ym 1996 drwy eu cynnyrch blaenllaw, ffa soia Roundup Ready. Arweiniodd y PCBs a gynhyrchwyd gan Monsanto at halogiad amgylcheddol eang, gydag effeithiau dinistriol ar gymunedau lleol. Roedd Monsanto'n gweithredu ffatri weithgynhyrchu PCB yn Anniston, UDA rhwng 1929 a 1971, gan ddympio gwastraff gwenwynig i ddyfrffyrdd lleol. Arweiniodd yr halogiad at gyfraddau uchel o ganser, clefyd yr afu a diabetes yn sgil yr halogiad, a llygrodd y pridd a'r systemau dŵr. Datgelodd profion fod y lefelau PCB 200 gwaith yn uwch na'r terfyn diogelwch ffederal mewn nentydd lleol. Mae dogfennau mewnol yn datgelu bod Monsanto'n gwybod am beryglon PCB mor gynnar â 1937, ond wedi parhau i'w gynhyrchu tan 1977. Claddodd y cwmni bridd halogedig mewn safleoedd tirlenwi heb eu leinio. Yn 2003, talodd Monsanto $700 miliwn i setlo hawliadau gan 20,000 o drigolion Anniston yn sgil halogiad PCB. Mae hanes degawdau o gamymddwyn corfforaethol Monsanto wedi gadael marc parhaol ar iechyd y cyhoedd, diogelwch amgylcheddol ac annibyniaeth amaethyddol. O effeithiau dinistriol Agent Orange i'r ddadl barhaus ynghylch Roundup, mae eu gweithredoedd yn parhau i effeithio ar filiynau o fywydau ledled y byd.

Nid yw'r ffaith bod Bayer wedi eu caffael—rhywbeth rwy'n siŵr eu bod yn difaru—wedi lleddfu gwaddol cythryblus y cwmni, wrth i achosion cyfreithiol a phryderon iechyd barhau. Fe welwch fod stori Monsanto'n atgoffa'n glir sut y mae elw corfforaethol yn aml yn cael blaenoriaeth dros les y cyhoedd. Ym 1919, aeth y cwmni cemegol o'r Unol Daleithiau Monsanto i bartneriaeth â gweithfeydd cemegol Graesser yng Nghefn-mawr i gynhyrchu fanilin, asid salisylig, asbrin, a chemegau prosesu rwber yn nes ymlaen. Yn ddiweddarach, gweithredwyd y safle gan Flexsys, un o is-gwmnïau Solutia, ond daeth cynhyrchiant i ben yn 2010.

Ceir honiadau eang fod PCBs, cemegau gwenwynig nad ydynt yn dadelfennu ond sy'n cronni yn yr amgylchedd, ac mewn anifeiliaid, pysgod a bodau dynol dros amser, wedi cael eu dympio. Cafodd y cemegau hyn eu dympio mewn 12 safle y gwyddys amdanynt ledled Cymru, gan gynnwys yn Rhiwabon, Cefn-mawr a lagŵn tar asid Llwyneinion ger Rhosllanerchrugog. Mae tystiolaeth a gasglwyd gan ymgyrchwyr ac arbenigwyr dros flynyddoedd yn honni y gallai PCBs fod wedi bod yn gyfrifol am gynnydd yn nifer y canserau prin yn yr ardaloedd hynny. Datgelodd preswylydd lleol, a ymddangosodd ar Buried gyda Michael Sheen, sef Michael Phillips, ei fod ef a'i ffrindiau pan oeddent yn blant wedi mynd i lawr at lagŵn asid Llwyneinion i wylio wrth i griwiau tân frwydro i ddod â thân yno dan reolaeth ym 1980. Cymerodd 18 awr i ddiffodd y tân, ond flynyddoedd yn ddiweddarach, cafodd Michael a'i ffrindiau i gyd ganserau prin y mae'n eu priodoli i gysylltiad â PCBs. Ac mae'n dweud, 'Dywedodd fy llawfeddyg, "Mae hyn yn rhyfedd, nid wyf erioed wedi gweld y math hwn o ganser o'r blaen" ac roedd wedi cael gyrfa nodedig dros 40 mlynedd', meddai Phillips. Mae dau o'i ffrindiau wedi marw, gyda chanser yr ymennydd a chanser y fron. Mae un arall yn brwydro yn erbyn canser yr ymennydd, tra bod pedwerydd wedi cael tynnu ei holl nodau lymff, gan fod canser ynddynt. Roedd gan bumed yr un math o ganser â Phillips—rhywbeth y dywedodd ei lawfeddyg ei fod yn cyfateb o ran tebygolrwydd i ennill y loteri bob dydd am chwe mis.

A dyna'r realiti heddiw ynghylch y sefyllfa a adawyd ar ôl gan y gwaethaf o gyfalafiaeth ryngwladol. Yn y pen draw, mae'n ymwneud â phobl, â'u hamgylchedd a'n hamgylchedd ninnau. Mae'n ymwneud â'r bygythiadau posibl iddynt hwy, eu teuluoedd, eu plant a chenedlaethau'r dyfodol. A dyna pam ei bod yn ddyletswydd arnom i fynnu gweithredu a rhoi fframwaith strategol a chynllun gweithredu ar waith. Diolch yn fawr.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 5. Dadl Aelodau o dan Reol Sefydlog 11.21(iv): Tir halogedig
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 5. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Contaminated land

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 5. Dadl Aelodau o dan Reol Sefydlog 11.21(iv): Tir halogedig
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 5. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Contaminated land
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Can I begin by thanking Niamh, with Elwyn's support, for bringing this important issue to the Chamber today? Some of what I'm going to say may repeat some things that Niamh and Elwyn have said, but that's because they are important and need to be said more than once.

Wales has a proud industrial history. It has brought jobs and prosperity to communities across the country and made an enormous contribution to the development of modern Britain. But that history has also left us with problems, which, many decades later, we are still having to deal with. Old mines, quarries, chemical works and industrial sites simply did not operate to the environmental standards that we would expect today. And for some of the people I represent, that isn't just history. Close to the north-eastern border of my constituency, as mentioned by Elwyn, near Rhos, Cefn Mawr, Acrefair and Ruabon, is the former Monsanto chemical waste tip. This is not rumour or local folklore. Parliamentary records confirm that Monsanto chemicals were deposited there in 1964 and 1965—prior to my being born, just.

More than 60 years later, people are still asking questions about that site and the neighbouring acid tar lagoon. Wrexham council has investigated the sites extensively. Its position is that contaminants are present, but the sites do not meet the legal definition of contaminated land. It does, however, continue to inspect and monitor them. But I can understand why people living nearby remain concerned. If you live close to somewhere like this, you want straightforward answers. What is in the ground? Is it getting out? Is there any risk to my family or my home, and if there is a problem, who is going to do something about it? These seem perfectly reasonable questions to me, and 60 years is an awfully long time to be asking them.

There have been calls for people living near contaminated sites to be offered blood tests for PCBs. Public Health Wales has considered that, and its advice is that blood testing is not recommended. It cannot reliably tell somebody how or where they were exposed, or what the consequences for their health might be. We should listen to that advice. There's little point in offering people a test that may leave them with more questions rather than fewer.

But that makes investigating the land itself all the more important. We need to establish what is actually there, whether contaminants are escaping and whether they present a genuine risk. This is where councils need help. They have responsibilities for contaminated land, but investigating sites like these is complicated and expensive. I welcome the fact that capital funding has now been agreed, but Wrexham County Borough Council is already making the point that additional funding will be needed if councils are going to investigate potentially contaminated sites properly. I think we should listen to them. There is little use giving local authorities responsibility for dealing with these sites if we don't also give them the means to do the job.

Then, of course, comes, as Niamh has mentioned, the difficult question of who pays if something needs putting right. Where the original polluter can be identified and liability established, every reasonable effort should be made to recover the costs from them. But when something happened 50, 60 or even 100 years ago, that isn't always possible. Companies disappear, businesses change hands and records are lost. We cannot simply shrug our shoulders. The fact that pollution is old doesn't make it any less real. And it isn't reasonable to leave one council and its council tax payers facing an enormous bill simply because the original polluter can no longer be pursued. There is a balance to be struck here.

I don't want to frighten people unnecessarily. Public Health Wales makes clear that PCBs can come from a number of sources and that finding elevated levels in a particular place does not necessarily establish where someone has been exposed. What I do want is for people to have confidence that somebody is actually finding out. If a site is safe, tell them, give them reassurance. If there's a problem, tell them and then do something about it.

The people living near the former Monsanto tip have lived with questions about that site for long enough. There will be other communities across Wales in very much the same position. They deserve answers, they deserve a system capable of establishing the facts, and where action is needed, they deserve to know that the money and the determination are there to see it through. As their representatives, the least we can do is to make sure their questions are heard and keep asking them until they get a proper answer. Thank you.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
A gaf i ddechrau drwy ddiolch i Niamh, gyda chefnogaeth Elwyn, am ddod â'r mater pwysig hwn i'r Siambr heddiw? Efallai y bydd rhywfaint o'r hyn rwy'n mynd i'w ddweud yn ailadrodd rhai pethau y mae Niamh ac Elwyn wedi'u dweud, ond mae hynny'n dangos eu bod yn bwysig, ac mae angen eu dweud fwy nag unwaith.

Mae gan Gymru hanes diwydiannol balch. Mae wedi dod â swyddi a ffyniant i gymunedau ledled y wlad ac wedi gwneud cyfraniad enfawr at ddatblygiad y Brydain fodern. Ond mae'r hanes hwnnw hefyd dod â phroblemau yn ei sgil rydym yn dal i orfod delio â nhw ddegawdau lawer yn ddiweddarach. Nid oedd hen fwyngloddiau, chwareli, gweithfeydd cemegol a safleoedd diwydiannol yn gweithredu i'r safonau amgylcheddol y byddem yn eu disgwyl heddiw. Ac i rai o'r bobl rwy'n eu cynrychioli, nid hanes yn unig yw hynny. Yn agos at ffin ogledd-ddwyreiniol fy etholaeth, fel y soniodd Elwyn, ger Rhos, Cefn-mawr, Acre-fair a Rhiwabon, mae hen domen wastraff cemegol Monsanto. Nid sibrydion na llên gwerin leol yw hyn. Mae cofnodion seneddol yn cadarnhau bod cemegau Monsanto wedi'u ollwng yno ym 1964 a 1965—cyn imi gael fy ngeni, o drwch blewyn.

Dros 60 mlynedd yn ddiweddarach, mae pobl yn dal i ofyn cwestiynau am y safle hwnnw a'r lagŵn tar asid cyfagos. Mae cyngor Wrecsam wedi ymchwilio'n helaeth i'r safleoedd. Eu safbwynt nhw yw bod halogion yn bresennol, ond nad yw'r safleoedd yn bodloni'r diffiniad cyfreithiol o dir halogedig. Fodd bynnag, mae'n parhau i'w harchwilio a'u monitro. Ond gallaf ddeall pam y mae pobl sy'n byw gerllaw yn parhau i fod yn bryderus. Os ydych chi'n byw'n agos at rywle fel hyn, rydych chi eisiau atebion plaen. Beth sydd yn y ddaear? A yw'n dod allan? A oes unrhyw berygl i fy nheulu neu fy nghartref, ac os oes problem, pwy sy'n mynd i wneud rhywbeth yn ei chylch? Mae'r rhain yn swnio fel cwestiynau cwbl resymol i mi, ac mae 60 mlynedd yn amser hir iawn i fod yn eu gofyn.

Mae galwadau wedi bod i gynnig profion gwaed ar gyfer PCBs i bobl sy'n byw ger safleoedd halogedig. Mae Iechyd Cyhoeddus Cymru wedi ystyried hynny, a'u cyngor nhw yw na ddylid argymell profion gwaed. Ni allant ddweud yn ddibynadwy wrth rywun sut neu ble y daethant i gysylltiad â PCBs, neu ba ganlyniadau y gallai hynny ei olygu i'w hiechyd. Dylem wrando ar y cyngor hwnnw. Nid oes fawr o bwynt cynnig prawf i bobl a allai arwain at fwy o gwestiynau yn hytrach na llai.

Ond mae hynny'n gwneud ymchwilio i'r tir ei hun yn bwysicach fyth. Mae angen inni sefydlu beth sydd yno mewn gwirionedd, a yw halogion yn dianc ac a ydynt yn achosi risg wirioneddol. Dyma lle mae angen cymorth ar gynghorau. Mae ganddynt gyfrifoldebau am dir halogedig, ond mae ymchwilio i safleoedd fel y rhain yn gymhleth ac yn ddrud. Rwy'n croesawu'r ffaith bod cyllid cyfalaf bellach wedi'i gytuno, ond mae Cyngor Bwrdeistref Sirol Wrecsam eisoes yn gwneud y pwynt y bydd angen cyllid ychwanegol os yw cynghorau'n mynd i archwilio safleoedd halogedig posibl yn briodol. Credaf y dylem wrando arnynt. Nid oes llawer o bwynt rhoi cyfrifoldeb i awdurdodau lleol am ddelio â'r safleoedd hyn os nad ydym hefyd yn rhoi'r dulliau gweithredu iddynt wneud y gwaith.

Yna, wrth gwrs, fel y mae Niamh wedi sôn, mae'r cwestiwn anodd o bwy sy'n talu os oes angen unioni rhywbeth. Lle gellir canfod pwy yw'r llygrwr gwreiddiol a sefydlu atebolrwydd, dylid gwneud pob ymdrech resymol i adennill y costau ganddynt. Ond pan ddigwyddodd rhywbeth 50, 60 neu hyd yn oed 100 mlynedd yn ôl, nid yw hynny bob amser yn bosibl. Mae cwmnïau'n diflannu, mae busnesau'n newid dwylo ac mae cofnodion yn cael eu colli. Ni allwn anwybyddu'r broblem. Nid yw'r ffaith bod llygredd yn hen yn ei wneud yn llai real. Ac nid yw'n rhesymol gadael un cyngor a thalwyr ei dreth gyngor i wynebu bil enfawr am na ellir mynd ar ôl y llygrwr gwreiddiol mwyach. Mae angen taro cydbwysedd.

Nid wyf eisiau dychryn pobl yn ddiangen. Mae Iechyd Cyhoeddus Cymru yn nodi'n glir y gall PCBs ddod o nifer o ffynonellau ac nad yw canfod lefelau uchel mewn lle penodol o reidrwydd yn sefydlu ble y daeth rhywun i gysylltiad â nhw. Yr hyn rwyf ei eisiau yw i bobl fod yn hyderus fod rhywun yn canfod y gwir. Os yw safle'n ddiogel, dywedwch wrthynt, rhowch sicrwydd iddynt. Os oes problem, dywedwch wrthynt ac yna gwnewch rywbeth yn ei chylch.

Mae'r bobl sy'n byw ger hen domen Monsanto wedi byw gyda chwestiynau ynglŷn â'r safle hwnnw ers digon o amser. Bydd cymunedau eraill ledled Cymru yn yr un sefyllfa. Maent yn haeddu atebion, maent yn haeddu system sy'n gallu sefydlu'r ffeithiau, a lle mae angen gweithredu, maent yn haeddu gwybod bod yr arian a'r penderfyniad yno i'w wneud. Fel eu cynrychiolwyr, y peth lleiaf y gallwn ei wneud yw sicrhau bod eu cwestiynau'n cael eu clywed a pharhau i'w gofyn hyd nes y cânt ateb iawn. Diolch.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 5. Dadl Aelodau o dan Reol Sefydlog 11.21(iv): Tir halogedig
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 5. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Contaminated land
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Can I welcome this debate and thank those who have already spoken? There have been some powerful contributions so far. It is obviously the subject of enormous cause for concern across Wales, including in and near my constituency, and indeed in my home village of Ruabon. I support the motion, obviously. I must say, though, that I would have liked to have seen greater reference to the role of the Welsh Government in addressing land contamination in Wales and in terms of protecting public health. There is historic precedent for the Welsh Government to intervene with money. I'll come to that in a moment, though.

First, my thanks must go to Michael Sheen and his production team for highlighting this issue, and also to Steve Witherden MP and his wife, Councillor Katie Witherden. These are activists who are featured in Michael Sheen's documentary, and Steve, in particular, has been very vocal in Parliament on the subject. He's raised the need for Natural Resources Wales to undertake urgent tests. Furthermore, Public Health Wales must undertake a programme of blood testing in affected areas without delay. It is the Welsh Government that must lead on this matter and get to grips with it, not shirk responsibility.

Turning to those who pay, I don't think that anybody in this Chamber would disagree that the polluter should pay. Absolutely, those responsible should be held to account and should pay for what they have done. But this is often not possible, sadly. And here comes the historic precedent. Back in 2015, contaminated land issues hit the headlines in north Wales, in Coedpoeth, in my constituency, and also in Blanefield up in Scotland. In both cases, the polluters sadly no longer existed, and so in the case of Scotland, it was the UK Government and Stirling Council who paid. The Scottish Government did not contribute. In contrast, here in Wales, to remediate the land in Coedpoeth, it was the Welsh Government that paid. The UK Government did not contribute. And then in this decade, it was the Welsh Government that pledged £100 million for coal-tip remediation, with an additional £143 million from the UK Labour Government.

What these recent major cases requiring Government help demonstrate above all is that all levels of government—all levels of government—need to act fast and need to act together in partnership. That's why there is a need for a consistent approach and, indeed, a framework, as the motion calls for. So, I support the motion, but I would urge the Government here in Wales to have a more responsible role within that framework and to do as we did in Government to help solve the problem, not to pass the problem to councils or to Westminster. Councils, citizens, communities cannot afford the cost of remediation, nor can they afford to wait any longer for action. So, I call on the Government here to stand up for the people of Wales by taking urgent action where it can, now.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
A gaf i groesawu'r ddadl hon a diolch i'r rhai sydd eisoes wedi siarad? Cafwyd cyfraniadau pwerus hyd yn hyn. Mae'n amlwg ei fod yn destun pryder enfawr ledled Cymru, gan gynnwys yn fy etholaeth i a'r cyffiniau, ac yn wir yn fy mhentref enedigol, Rhiwabon. Rwy'n cefnogi'r cynnig, yn amlwg. Rhaid imi ddweud, fodd bynnag, y buaswn wedi hoffi gweld mwy o gyfeirio at rôl Llywodraeth Cymru yn mynd i'r afael â halogi tir yng Nghymru ac o ran diogelu iechyd y cyhoedd. Mae cynsail hanesyddol i Lywodraeth Cymru ymyrryd gydag arian. Ond fe ddof at hynny mewn eiliad.

Yn gyntaf, rhaid diolch i Michael Sheen a'i dîm cynhyrchu am dynnu sylw at y mater hwn, ac i Steve Witherden AS a'i wraig, y Cynghorydd Katie Witherden. Mae'r rhain yn ymgyrchwyr sy'n ymddangos yn rhaglen ddogfen Michael Sheen, ac mae Steve yn enwedig wedi bod yn llafar iawn yn y Senedd ar y pwnc. Mae wedi codi'r angen i Cyfoeth Naturiol Cymru gynnal profion brys. Ar ben hynny, rhaid i Iechyd Cyhoeddus Cymru gynnal rhaglen o brofion gwaed yn yr ardaloedd yr effeithir arnynt yn ddi-oed. Rhaid i Lywodraeth Cymru arwain ar y mater hwn a mynd i'r afael ag ef, nid osgoi cyfrifoldeb.

Gan droi at y rhai sy'n talu, nid wyf yn credu y byddai unrhyw un yn y Siambr hon yn anghytuno y dylai'r llygrwr dalu. Yn hollol, dylai'r rhai sy'n gyfrifol gael eu dwyn i gyfrif a dylent dalu am yr hyn y maent wedi'i wneud. Ond yn aml, nid yw hyn yn bosibl yn anffodus. A dyma'r cynsail hanesyddol. Yn ôl yn 2015, daeth materion tir halogedig i'r penawdau yng ngogledd Cymru, yng Nghoed-poeth, yn fy etholaeth i, a hefyd yn Blanefield yn yr Alban. Yn y ddau achos, nid oedd y llygrwyr yn bodoli mwyach, ac felly, yn achos yr Alban, Llywodraeth y DU a Chyngor Stirling a dalodd. Ni chafwyd cyfraniad gan Lywodraeth yr Alban. Mewn cyferbyniad, yma yng Nghymru, i adfer y tir yng Nghoed-poeth, Llywodraeth Cymru a dalodd. Ni chafwyd cyfraniad gan Lywodraeth y DU. Ac yna yn y degawd hwn, Llywodraeth Cymru a addawodd £100 miliwn ar gyfer adfer tomenni glo, gyda £143 miliwn ychwanegol gan Lywodraeth Lafur y DU.

Yr hyn y mae'r achosion mawr diweddar hyn sy'n galw am gymorth Llywodraeth yn ei ddangos yn anad dim yw bod angen i bob lefel o lywodraeth—pob lefel o lywodraeth—weithredu'n gyflym a bod angen iddynt weithredu gyda'i gilydd mewn partneriaeth. Dyna pam y mae angen dull cyson o weithredu, a fframwaith yn wir, fel y mae'r cynnig yn galw amdano. Felly, rwy'n cefnogi'r cynnig, ond rwy'n annog y Llywodraeth yma yng Nghymru i gael rôl fwy cyfrifol o fewn y fframwaith hwnnw ac i wneud fel y gwnaethom ni pan oeddem yn Llywodraeth i helpu i ddatrys y broblem, nid trosglwyddo'r broblem i gynghorau neu i San Steffan. Ni all cynghorau, dinasyddion, cymunedau fforddio cost adfer, ac ni allant fforddio aros yn hirach cyn i weithredu ddigwydd. Felly, galwaf ar y Llywodraeth yma i sefyll dros bobl Cymru drwy roi camau brys ar waith lle y gall, a gwneud hynny nawr.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 5. Dadl Aelodau o dan Reol Sefydlog 11.21(iv): Tir halogedig
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 5. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Contaminated land
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Thanks, Niamh, for bringing this debate forward. This subject of contaminated land and pollution in our water supply is unfortunately a frequent topic in this Senedd Chamber and has been over the past number of years. Now, we have a new Plaid Cymru Government, and certainly when I was on the committee with Llyr Gruffydd as our Chair in the environment committee, this was a very big issue for us as a committee. And it's nice to see Carolyn Thomas up there, a former colleague of ours here in the Senedd, who also used to speak up very passionately and very strongly about contaminated land. Thank you, Carolyn.

I strongly believe that in incidents involving contamination, leaks or the illegal dumping of waste, the perpetrator should be held responsible and required to cover the cost of clearing and restoring the site. This is especially important in cases that involve repeat offenders, such as Dave Neal. My colleague Paul Davies, over the years, has represented so many constituents who were badly affected, so much so that they used to have to keep their windows closed, and yet for years it went on and on and on. Fines aren't enough. Many of these environmental polluters simply add them as a business cost because the fines—. They make more money doing what they do than the cost of a fine, and it's wrong.

We must take a stronger stance against illegal dumping that contaminates our land and threatens our natural environment. Failure to take stronger action against these criminals has even brought down a former First Minister here. Accepting funding from individuals involved in this activity was shameful. So, I reiterate my call for stronger action to be taken against these organisations and for a clear message to be sent out today that this behaviour cannot and will not be allowed to continue. You pollute our land in Wales and you will pay.

In a freedom of information request conducted by Friends of the Earth, it was found that potentially over 45,000 contaminated land sites exist in Wales, yet only 82 sites are designated as contaminated. So, data collection and investigations and inspections are key. Only six out of our 22 councils provide a full public register online. Fifteen councils have an inspection strategy, but only four have updated it in the last five years. I'm sorry, but you need to really get a grip of this. These figures are deeply concerning, especially as we all know that contaminated land can have a significant impact on our health, our environment and our water supplies. Today, there have been some shocking examples of illnesses that people have contracted—some terminal—and we cannot stand by any more. And I thank the people in the gallery for the work that you do. You're not elected; you're volunteers, you're activists against these environmental criminals.

It is vital that these sites and other potential sites of contaminated land are reviewed, monitored and registered. This will ensure that we have current and up-to-date figures, allowing contamination to be identified and contained as effectively as possible. It is essential that joint action is taken by the Welsh and UK Governments, and appropriate resources to identify, assess, monitor and register are key. We also need to ensure that responsibility does not simply fall on local authorities and taxpayers when pollution has been caused by those who have chosen to break the law. Where wrongdoing can be established, those responsible should face appropriate enforcement and be required to contribute towards the costs of remediation. And if you think that a fine is enough, it isn't. If you keep polluting, you should go to prison.

The public should not be left to carry the financial burden of dealing with pollution caused by illegal activity. There must also be greater transparency around contaminated land. Communities should be able to understand where these sites are located, what risks have been identified, what action is being taken and whether that action is satisfactory. Regular inspections and up-to-date public registers would help. We must ensure that lessons are learned from previous incidents. Where contamination occurs, the response should be timely, co-ordinated and proportionate, with clear responsibility for investigating the source.

This is not simply about dealing with contamination after it has occurred; it is about prevention, enforcement and accountability. If we really are serious about protecting our land, our water supplies, our environment and the health of our people, then we must ensure that contaminated land is dealt with. Those who illegally dump waste or cause contamination must understand that there are serious consequences.

I'll just say this: I would like the First Minister now—. And I am not calling for any further devolution, but I've called for this numerous times before. Currently, any fines from environmental pollution go to the UK Treasury. That is morally wrong. That money should come to Wales. So, do your best, First Minister; you will have my support. That money should come to help to pay for the pollution. But let you now, as the new Plaid Government, work with us all, because we're all against allowing these criminals to pollute. Diolch yn fawr iawn.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Diolch am gyflwyno'r ddadl hon, Niamh. Yn anffodus, mae mater tir halogedig a llygredd yn ein cyflenwad dŵr yn bwnc sy'n codi'n aml yn y Siambr y Senedd hon ac mae wedi gwneud hynny dros y blynyddoedd diwethaf. Nawr, mae gennym Lywodraeth Plaid Cymru, ac yn sicr pan oeddwn i ar y pwyllgor gyda Llyr Gruffydd fel ein Cadeirydd yn y pwyllgor amgylchedd, roedd hwn yn fater mawr iawn i ni fel pwyllgor. Ac mae'n braf gweld Carolyn Thomas i fyny yno, cyn gyd-Aelod i ni yma yn y Senedd, un arall oedd yn arfer siarad yn angerddol ac yn gryf iawn am dir halogedig. Diolch, Carolyn.

Rwy'n credu'n gryf y dylid dwyn y troseddwr i gyfrif mewn digwyddiadau sy'n ymwneud â halogi, gollyngiadau neu ddympio gwastraff yn anghyfreithlon, a dylai fod yn ofynnol iddo dalu'r gost am glirio ac adfer y safle. Mae hyn yn arbennig o bwysig mewn achosion yn ymwneud â throseddwyr mynych, fel Dave Neal. Dros y blynyddoedd, mae fy nghyd-Aelod Paul Davies wedi cynrychioli cymaint o etholwyr a gafodd eu heffeithio'n wael, cymaint felly nes eu bod yn arfer gorfod cadw eu ffenestri ar gau, ac eto am flynyddoedd aeth ymlaen ac ymlaen ac ymlaen. Nid yw dirwyon yn ddigon. Bydd llawer o'r llygrwyr amgylcheddol hyn yn eu cyfrif fel cost busnes am fod y dirwyon—. Maent yn gwneud mwy o arian yn gwneud yr hyn a wnânt na'r hyn a dalant yn ddirwy, ac mae'n anghywir.

Rhaid inni sefyll yn gryfach yn erbyn dympio anghyfreithlon sy'n halogi ein tir ac yn bygwth ein hamgylchedd naturiol. Arweiniodd methiant i roi camau cryfach ar waith yn erbyn y troseddwyr hyn at wneud i gyn-Brif Weinidog yma golli ei swydd. Roedd derbyn cyllid gan unigolion a oedd yn rhan o'r gweithgaredd hwn yn gywilyddus. Felly, rwy'n ailadrodd fy ngalwad am weithredu'n gryfach yn erbyn y sefydliadau hyn ac anfon neges glir heddiw na ellir ac na fydd yr ymddygiad hwn yn cael ei ganiatáu i barhau. Os ydych chi'n llygru ein tir yng Nghymru, fe fyddwch chi'n talu am hynny.

Mewn cais rhyddid gwybodaeth gan Cyfeillion y Ddaear, canfuwyd bod dros 45,000 o safleoedd tir halogedig posibl yn bodoli yng Nghymru, ond dim ond 82 o safleoedd a ddynodwyd fel rhai halogedig. Felly, mae casglu data ac ymchwiliadau ac arolygiadau yn allweddol. Dim ond chwech o'n 22 cyngor sy'n darparu cofrestr gyhoeddus lawn ar-lein. Mae gan 15 cyngor strategaeth arolygu, ond dim ond pedwar sydd wedi ei diweddaru yn y pum mlynedd diwethaf. Mae'n ddrwg gennyf, ond mae angen ichi fynd i'r afael o ddifrif â hyn. Mae'r ffigurau'n peri pryder mawr, yn enwedig gan ein bod i gyd yn gwybod y gall tir halogedig effeithio'n sylweddol ar ein hiechyd, ein hamgylchedd a'n cyflenwadau dŵr. Heddiw, cafwyd enghreifftiau brawychus o salwch a ddioddefwyd gan bobl—salwch angheuol mewn rhai achosion—ac ni allwn gicio ein sodlau mwyach. Ac rwy'n diolch i'r bobl yn yr oriel am y gwaith rydych chi'n ei wneud. Nid ydych chi'n cael eich ethol; gwirfoddolwyr ydych chi, ymgyrchwyr yn erbyn y troseddwyr amgylcheddol hyn.

Mae'n hanfodol fod y safleoedd hyn a safleoedd tir halogedig posibl eraill yn cael eu hadolygu, eu monitro a'u cofrestru. Bydd hyn yn sicrhau bod gennym ffigurau cyfredol, i ganiatáu i halogiad gael ei nodi a'i gynnwys mor effeithiol â phosibl. Mae'n hanfodol fod Llywodraeth Cymru a'r DU yn gweithredu ar y cyd, ac mae adnoddau priodol i nodi, asesu, monitro a chofrestru yn allweddol. Mae angen inni sicrhau hefyd nad yw'r cyfrifoldeb yn disgyn ar awdurdodau lleol a threthdalwyr pan fydd llygredd wedi'i achosi gan rai sydd wedi dewis torri'r gyfraith. Lle gellir sefydlu trosedd, dylai'r rhai sy'n gyfrifol wynebu camau gorfodi priodol a bod gofyn iddynt gyfrannu tuag at gostau adfer. Ac os ydych chi'n meddwl bod dirwy'n ddigon, nid yw hynny'n wir. Os ydych chi'n parhau i lygru, dylech gael eich carcharu.

Ni ddylid gadael i'r cyhoedd ysgwyddo'r baich ariannol o ddelio â llygredd a achosir gan weithgaredd anghyfreithlon. Rhaid cael mwy o dryloywder ynghylch tir halogedig. Dylai cymunedau allu deall ble mae'r safleoedd hyn wedi'u lleoli, pa risgiau a nodwyd, pa gamau sy'n cael eu cymryd ac a yw'r camau hynny'n foddhaol. Byddai arolygiadau rheolaidd a chofrestri cyhoeddus cyfredol yn helpu. Rhaid inni sicrhau bod gwersi'n cael eu dysgu o ddigwyddiadau blaenorol. Pan fydd halogiad yn digwydd, dylai'r ymateb fod yn amserol, yn gydgysylltiedig ac yn gymesur, gyda chyfrifoldeb clir am ymchwilio i'r ffynhonnell.

Nid mater syml o ddelio â halogiad ar ôl iddo ddigwydd yw hyn; mae'n ymwneud ag atal, gorfodi ac atebolrwydd. Os ydym o ddifrif am ddiogelu ein tir, ein cyflenwadau dŵr, ein hamgylchedd ac iechyd ein pobl, rhaid inni fynd i'r afael â thir halogedig. Rhaid i'r rhai sy'n dympio gwastraff yn anghyfreithlon neu'n achosi halogiad ddeall bod canlyniadau difrifol i hynny.

Fe ddywedaf hyn: hoffwn i'r Prif Weinidog nawr—. Ac nid wyf yn galw am unrhyw ddatganoli pellach, ond rwyf wedi galw am hyn sawl gwaith o'r blaen. Ar hyn o bryd, mae unrhyw ddirwyon yn sgil llygredd amgylcheddol yn mynd i Drysorlys y DU. Mae hynny'n foesol anghywir. Dylai'r arian hwnnw ddod i Gymru. Felly, gwnewch eich gorau, Brif Weinidog; fe gewch chi fy nghefnogaeth i. Dylai'r arian hwnnw ddod i helpu i dalu am y llygredd. Ond fel Llywodraeth newydd Plaid Cymru, gweithiwch gyda ni i gyd nawr, oherwydd mae pawb ohonom yn erbyn caniatáu i'r troseddwyr hyn lygru. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 5. Dadl Aelodau o dan Reol Sefydlog 11.21(iv): Tir halogedig
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 5. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Contaminated land
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
I want to thank Niamh Salkeld for bringing forward this important debate today, and also Elwyn Vaughan for his work on it as well, because like many people, I recently watched the Michael Sheen documentary on contaminated land, and I didn't really know what to expect, so I was horrified when pretty much straight away in the documentary it focuses on Brofiscin quarry near Groesfaen in my constituency of Caerdydd Penarth. The Environment Agency named this site one of the most polluted sites in Britain, with 67 different toxic chemicals, including seven different PCBs, leaking into the porous ground at the former limestone quarry.

Decades ago, people purchased homes in Groesfaen, unaware they were now living next to one of the most contaminated places in the whole of the UK. Children grew up there and played around the quarry, and for decades families were uninformed of the risks. In 2011, after decades of campaigning, the quarry was finally capped to prevent PCBs from leaking. So, although Brofiscin has been designated a contaminated site, thousands of sites are yet to be classified. Communities have the right to know if they're living next door to contaminated land, and they should not be left footing the bill for toxic waste clean-ups.

The site in Brofiscin immediately brought the issue home, because when we talk about contaminated land, it may sound like a historical issue, but these places exist right now all across Wales in our communities, where people live and work and walk and exercise and raise their families. I want to recognise the important work that has been done to remediate the site in my constituency, but I am aware this isn't the case for similar sites across Wales, and those responsible must be held to account and made to clean up. PCBs were banned decades ago, yet all across Wales you'll still find them. And because these chemicals persist for such a long time, we're now dealing with another legacy of the industrial past of Wales. We cannot change the past, but we can decide how we deal with the consequences. Polluters should pay, and if they won't or can't, Westminster needs to step up and introduce a funding mechanism to support investigations and remediation.

The motion rightly points out the absence of a clear and consistent national picture of potentially contaminated land across Wales, and I think this lack of a clear picture is causing fear unnecessarily in our communities. In Gwaelod-y-garth, there was recent flooding caused by blasting at a nearby quarry shortly before the release of this documentary. Residents were then understandably concerned that perhaps PCBs were involved in this case, which is why establishing this framework for testing and assessment of contaminated land is so crucial, so people feel informed and confident. And where there is credible concern, communities should be able to have the confidence that the site will be properly investigated and that the appropriate action is followed.

I think Brofiscin demonstrates the two sides to this issue. It demonstrates the scale of the industrial legacy that Wales has inherited, but it also demonstrates that we can do something about it, as Brofiscin underwent remediation in the early 2010s. Monsanto initially refused to contribute to clean-up. They said they'd hired a third-party waste disposal company to dump the chemicals, so they weren't responsible. But, fortunately, an agreement was eventually reached where they did contribute towards the clean-up.

The industrial history of Wales is something we should be proud of, but we also have a responsibility to deal properly with the environmental legacy it leaves, and never again should Wales be used as a dumping ground for toxic chemicals by large corporations. Diolch.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Hoffwn ddiolch i Niamh Salkeld am gyflwyno'r ddadl bwysig hon heddiw, a hefyd i Elwyn Vaughan am ei waith arni hefyd, oherwydd fel llawer o bobl, gwyliais raglen ddogfen Michael Sheen ar dir halogedig yn ddiweddar, ac nid oeddwn yn gwybod yn iawn beth i'w ddisgwyl, felly arswydais wrth weld bron yn syth yn y rhaglen ddogfen ei bod yn canolbwyntio ar chwarel Brofiscin ger y Groes-faen yn fy etholaeth i, Caerdydd Penarth. Enwodd Asiantaeth yr Amgylchedd y safle hwn yn un o'r safleoedd mwyaf llygredig ym Mhrydain, gyda 67 o wahanol gemegau gwenwynig, gan gynnwys saith PCB gwahanol, yn gollwng i'r ddaear fandyllog yn yr hen chwarel galchfaen.

Ddegawdau yn ôl, prynodd pobl gartrefi yn y Groes-faen, heb wybod eu bod bellach yn byw ger un o'r lleoedd mwyaf halogedig yn y DU gyfan. Tyfodd plant i fyny yno a chwarae o gwmpas y chwarel, ac am ddegawdau nid oedd teuluoedd yn gwybod am y risgiau. Yn 2011, ar ôl degawdau o ymgyrchu, cafodd y chwarel ei chapio o'r diwedd i atal PCBs rhag gollwng. Felly, er bod Brofiscin wedi'i ddynodi'n safle halogedig, mae miloedd o safleoedd eto i'w categoreiddio. Mae gan gymunedau hawl i wybod a ydynt yn byw drws nesaf i dir halogedig, ac ni ddylid eu gadael i dalu'r bil am lanhau gwastraff gwenwynig.

Roedd y safle yn chwarel Brofiscin yn crisialu'r mater yn syth, oherwydd pan fyddwn yn siarad am dir halogedig, efallai ei fod yn swnio fel mater hanesyddol, ond mae'r lleoedd hyn yn bodoli nawr ledled Cymru yn ein cymunedau, lle mae pobl yn byw ac yn gweithio ac yn cerdded ac yn ymarfer corff ac yn magu eu teuluoedd. Rwyf am gydnabod y gwaith pwysig sydd wedi'i wneud i adfer y safle yn fy etholaeth i, ond rwy'n ymwybodol nad yw hyn yn wir am safleoedd tebyg ledled Cymru, ac mae'n rhaid i'r rhai sy'n gyfrifol gael eu dwyn i gyfrif a'u gorfodi i lanhau. Cafodd PCBs eu gwahardd ddegawdau yn ôl, ond ledled Cymru maent i'w gweld o hyd. Ac oherwydd bod y cemegau hyn yn parhau am amser mor hir, rydym bellach yn delio â gwaddol arall o orffennol diwydiannol Cymru. Ni allwn newid y gorffennol, ond gallwn benderfynu sut rydym yn delio â'r canlyniadau. Dylai llygrwyr dalu, ac os na wnânt neu os na allant, mae angen i San Steffan gamu i'r adwy a chyflwyno mecanwaith ariannu i gefnogi ymchwiliadau a gwaith adfer.

Mae'r cynnig yn nodi'n gywir nad oes darlun cenedlaethol clir a chyson o dir a allai fod wedi'i halogi ledled Cymru, ac rwy'n credu bod diffyg darlun clir o'r fath yn achosi ofn diangen yn ein cymunedau. Yng Ngwaelod-y-garth, achoswyd llifogydd yn ddiweddar gan ffrwydriadau mewn chwarel gyfagos ychydig cyn darlledu'r rhaglen ddogfen hon. Roedd hi'n ddealladwy wedyn fod trigolion yn pryderu efallai fod PCBs wedi'u rhyddhau yn y digwyddiad hwnnw, a dyna pam y mae sefydlu'r fframwaith ar gyfer profi ac asesu tir halogedig mor hanfodol, fel bod pobl yn teimlo'n wybodus ac yn hyderus. Ac os oes lle i bryderu, dylai cymunedau allu bod yn hyderus y bydd y safle'n cael ei archwilio'n briodol a bod camau priodol yn cael eu dilyn.

Rwy'n credu bod Brofiscin yn dangos y ddwy ochr i'r mater hwn. Mae'n dangos graddau'r gwaddol diwydiannol y mae Cymru wedi'i etifeddu, ond mae hefyd yn dangos y gallwn wneud rhywbeth yn ei gylch, gan fod Brofiscin wedi cael ei adfer yn gynnar yn y 2010au. Ar y dechrau fe wrthododd Monsanto gyfrannu at y gwaith glanhau. Roeddent yn dweud eu bod wedi llogi cwmni gwaredu gwastraff trydydd parti i ddympio'r cemegau, ac felly, nad nhw oedd yn gyfrifol. Ond yn ffodus, daethant i gytundeb yn y pen draw i gyfrannu tuag at y gwaith glanhau.

Mae hanes diwydiannol Cymru yn rhywbeth y dylem fod yn falch ohono, ond mae gennym gyfrifoldeb hefyd i ddelio'n briodol â'r gwaddol amgylcheddol a adawodd ar ôl, ac ni ddylid defnyddio Cymru byth eto fel lle i ddympio cemegau gwenwynig gan gorfforaethau mawr. Diolch.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 5. Dadl Aelodau o dan Reol Sefydlog 11.21(iv): Tir halogedig
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 5. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Contaminated land
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
My thanks to Niamh for brining this motion forward. I speak in strong support of this motion, but, more importantly, to inject some practical, commonsense and local reality into a debate that goes straight to the heart of public health in Wales, and local accountability right across Wales too. I'd also like to thank Ken Skates for what he said about our area. As Ken knows, we live in one of the most heavily industrialised areas in north Wales, and it's got a huge historical legacy. I'll tell you about that in a moment.

What's buried under our soil doesn't simply disappear. Historic industrial pollution poses severe, as we've mentioned already, long-term risks to human health, animal welfare and our waterways, and the families living along those waterways too. My constituency, and that of Ken Skates and other people here within this Senedd, of Fflint Wrecsam goes right along the Dee estuary, and the industrial legacy is not an abstract concept there. And actually, dare I say it, it's not some inane lines in some academic briefing either. It's something we walk along and we see every day.

Let me tell you, I worked, years ago, as a beach guard, in a former life, as it were, a long time ago. I walked along the Dee estuary, along what's called the marsh there, from Flint castle all the way towards the steelworks. There was lots of industry along there. But one particular area used to be the site of Glanzstoff chemical works. Some people know about this. When I was a beach guard, I can remember walking there, and there were colours within the soil—there were pinks, oranges, awful alkalinity—which are there still to this day. So, if there's one thing I'd like to mention today, it's that that is a place they could look at, because you only have to take one dig with a shovel, and suddenly you've got bright colours. It looks fantastic, although it's covered in grass now, but underneath, it's a huge, awful legacy to the health of the people of the area. And worse still, it leaches straight into the river there, so that's awful.

The other thing I'd like to mention is if you cycle along the cycleway there—and Ken will probably tell you that, as well—at one stage there are pipes coming out of the ground where the old tip used to be. That's a real worry to those people in the area. So, I'd like to note this here today: make sure that people take that on board. And those are just two areas, to be honest. There's Courtaulds works that was there, there's the steelworks that was there. Lots of stuff has been dumped along that area. And places like this exist all over Wales.

A failure of national oversight is exactly what has been highlighted recently in the press and before the Welsh Affairs Committee, following investigations, as we've mentioned here today, by the BBC's Buried series. Analysis shows that, across Wales, there are tens of thousands of potentially contaminated sites and hundreds of areas that are classed as high risk. Yet the vast majority remain untested—as people have said—unmapped, and unmanaged. Hopefully, I've managed to map a couple of those places today. We can't continue with a postcode lottery where local councils and hard-pressed taxpayers are left holding the financial baby for historic industrial liabilities. Crucially, whilst we address the past, we must also stop creating tomorrow's contaminated land today. That's really important. That's why practical modern waste management and infrastructure is vital.

A couple of weeks ago, some of us visited the Enfinium Parc Adfer energy from waste facility on Deeside industrial park. Several people, I think, have been there, actually. There was a bit of historic apprehension to that facility because it was a bit concerning that it was regarded as an incinerator—'What would go into the skies?' We had no idea, really. But, having been there, the stewardship is absolutely fantastic, and stops, if you like, waste now being dumped into the environment, as we've seen in the past. I'd like to praise that company from here now. That's absolutely brilliant. That's what I would call practical environmentalism in action: dealing with unavoidable waste cleanly and domestically rather than burying liabilities or shipping waste overseas, which we've seen a lot of in recent times.

Turning directly to the motion before us, I fully endorse the core principles as set out: acknowledging the severe risks to human and animal health, recognising that liabilities fall unfairly on local communities, admitting the glaring absence of a clear national picture, addressing community uncertainty, and enforcing the vital polluter-pays principle so that the commercial polluters are made to pay wherever possible. But obviously, historically, that's not possible either.

I also acknowledge the work already undertaken by our local authorities and Natural Resources Wales under very difficult circumstances at times. Waste seems to be everywhere at times. Crucially, I support the calls to Government. Firstly, the Welsh Government must work with the UK Government to ensure polluters pay and introduce a dedicated ring-fenced funding mechanism to remediate historic sites where costs cannot be recovered from defunct operators.

Secondly, and most importantly, we must establish a comprehensive national framework for the testing and assessment of potentially contaminated land, prioritising those sites that pose the greatest risk, such as the areas I've just mentioned now, especially when they're leaching into our waterways, and provide real, tangible support to our local authorities so that they can finally fulfil their statutory responsibilities. We cannot leave local councils, our communities, and our taxpayers, more importantly, facing the costs and health hazards of pollution they did not cause—
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Diolch i Niamh am gyflwyno'r cynnig hwn. Rwy'n siarad yn gryf o blaid y cynnig hwn, ond yn bwysicach fyth, rwyf am chwistrellu rhywfaint o synnwyr cyffredin ymarferol a realiti lleol i mewn i ddadl sy'n mynd yn syth at galon iechyd cyhoeddus yng Nghymru, ac atebolrwydd lleol ledled Cymru hefyd. Hoffwn ddiolch i Ken Skates am yr hyn a ddywedodd am ein hardal. Fel y gŵyr Ken, rydym yn byw yn un o'r ardaloedd mwyaf diwydiannol yng ngogledd Cymru, ac mae ganddi waddol hanesyddol enfawr. Fe soniaf am hynny mewn eiliad.

Nid yw'r hyn sydd wedi'i gladdu o dan ein pridd yn diflannu. Fel y soniwyd eisoes, mae llygredd diwydiannol hanesyddol yn peri risgiau hirdymor difrifol i iechyd pobl, lles anifeiliaid a'n dyfrffyrdd, a'r teuluoedd sy'n byw ar hyd y dyfrffyrdd hynny. Mae fy etholaeth i, ac etholaeth Ken Skates a phobl eraill yma yn y Senedd hon, sef Fflint Wrecsam, yn rhedeg ar hyd aber afon Dyfrdwy, ac nid yw'r gwaddol diwydiannol yn gysyniad haniaethol yno. A dweud y gwir, os caf ddweud, nid brawddegau hurt mewn briff academaidd mohono chwaith. Mae'n rhywbeth rydym yn cerdded ar hyd-ddo ac yn ei weld bob dydd.

Gadewch i mi ddweud wrthych, flynyddoedd yn ôl, mewn bywyd blaenorol fel petai, amser maith yn ôl, roeddwn i'n gweithio fel gwarchodwr traeth. Roeddwn i'n cerdded ar hyd aber afon Dyfrdwy, ar hyd yr hyn a elwir yn gors yno, o gastell y Fflint yr holl ffordd tuag at y gwaith dur. Roedd llawer o ddiwydiant yno. Ond un ardal benodol ar y pryd oedd safle gwaith cemegol Glanzstoff. Mae rhai pobl yn gwybod am hyn. Pan oeddwn i'n warchodwr traeth, gallaf gofio cerdded yno, ac roedd lliwiau yn y pridd—roedd yna liwiau pinc, oren, alcalinedd ofnadwy—sy'n dal yno hyd heddiw. Felly, un peth yr hoffwn ei grybwyll heddiw, yw bod hwnnw'n safle y gallent edrych arno, gan mai dim ond un cloddiad â rhaw sydd angen i chi ei wneud, ac yn sydyn mae gennych chi liwiau llachar. Mae'n edrych yn wych, er ei fod wedi'i orchuddio â glaswellt nawr, ond oddi tano, mae'n waddol enfawr, erchyll i iechyd pobl yr ardal. Ac yn waeth byth, mae'n trwytholchi'n syth i'r afon yno, felly mae hynny'n ofnadwy.

Y peth arall yr hoffwn ei grybwyll os byddwch yn beicio ar hyd y llwybr beicio yno—ac mae'n debyg y bydd Ken yn dweud hyn wrthych chi hefyd—mewn un man mae pibellau'n dod allan o'r ddaear lle roedd yr hen domen yn arfer bod. Mae hynny'n bryder gwirioneddol i'r bobl yn yr ardal. Felly, hoffwn nodi hyn yma heddiw: gwnewch yn siŵr bod pobl yn rhoi sylw i hynny. A dau le yn unig yw'r rheini, i fod yn onest. Roedd yna waith Courtaulds yn arfer bod yno, a'r gwaith dur. Mae llawer o bethau wedi cael eu dympio ar hyd yr ardal honno. Ac mae llefydd fel hyn yn bodoli ledled Cymru.

Fel rydym wedi sôn yma heddiw, cafodd methiant goruchwyliaeth genedlaethol ei amlygu'n ddiweddar yn y wasg a gerbron y Pwyllgor Materion Cymreig, yn dilyn archwiliadau gan gyfres Buried y BBC. Mae dadansoddiadau'n dangos bod degau o filoedd o safleoedd a allai fod wedi'u halogi a channoedd o ardaloedd wedi'u categoreiddio fel rhai risg uchel. Eto i gyd, ni chynhaliwyd profion ar y mwyafrif helaeth ohonynt—fel y mae pobl wedi dweud—ac nid ydynt wedi'u mapio na'u rheoli. Gobeithio fy mod i wedi llwyddo i fapio un neu ddau o'r lleoedd hynny heddiw. Ni allwn barhau gyda loteri cod post lle mae cynghorau lleol a threthdalwyr dan bwysau'n cael eu gadael i dalu am gyfrifoldebau diwydiannol hanesyddol. Yn allweddol, wrth inni fynd i'r afael â'r gorffennol, rhaid inni hefyd roi'r gorau i greu tir halogedig yfory heddiw. Mae hynny'n bwysig iawn. Dyna pam y mae rheolaeth fodern ymarferol ar wastraff a seilwaith yn allweddol.

Ychydig wythnosau yn ôl, ymwelodd rhai ohonom â chyfleuster ynni o wastraff Parc Adfer Enfinium ym mharc diwydiannol Glannau Dyfrdwy. Rwy'n credu bod sawl un wedi bod yno. Roedd yna ychydig o bryder hanesyddol ynghlwm wrth y cyfleuster hwnnw am fod pobl braidd yn bryderus ei fod yn cael ei ystyried fel llosgydd—'Beth fyddai'n mynd i'r awyr?' Nid oedd gennym unrhyw syniad mewn gwirionedd. Ond ar ôl bod yno, mae'r stiwardiaeth yn hollol wych, a bellach yn atal gwastraff rhag cael ei ollwng i'r amgylchedd, fel oedd yn arfer digwydd yn y gorffennol. Hoffwn ganmol y cwmni hwnnw. Mae'n hollol wych. Dyna'r hyn y buaswn yn ei alw'n amgylcheddiaeth ymarferol ar waith: yn delio â gwastraff na ellir ei osgoi yn lân ac yn ddomestig yn hytrach na chladdu cyfrifoldebau neu gludo gwastraff dramor, fel sydd wedi bod yn digwydd yn aml yn ddiweddar.

Gan droi'n uniongyrchol at y cynnig sydd o'n blaenau, rwy'n cefnogi'r egwyddorion craidd fel y'u nodir yn llawn: cydnabod y risgiau difrifol i iechyd pobl ac anifeiliaid, cydnabod bod cyfrifoldebau'n disgyn yn annheg ar gymunedau lleol, cyfaddef absenoldeb amlwg darlun cenedlaethol clir, mynd i'r afael ag ansicrwydd cymunedol, a gorfodi'r egwyddor allweddol mai'r llygrwr sy'n talu fel bod llygrwyr masnachol yn cael eu gorfodi i dalu lle bynnag y bo modd. Ond yn amlwg, yn hanesyddol, nid yw hynny'n bosibl chwaith.

Rwyf hefyd yn cydnabod y gwaith sydd eisoes wedi'i wneud gan ein hawdurdodau lleol a Cyfoeth Naturiol Cymru mewn amgylchiadau anodd iawn ar adegau. Mae'n ymddangos bod gwastraff ym mhobman weithiau. Yn allweddol, rwy'n cefnogi'r galwadau ar Lywodraeth. Yn gyntaf, rhaid i Lywodraeth Cymru weithio gyda Llywodraeth y DU i sicrhau bod llygrwyr yn talu a chyflwyno mecanwaith ariannu pwrpasol wedi'i glustnodi ar gyfer adfer safleoedd hanesyddol lle na ellir adennill costau gan gwmnïau nad ydynt yn weithredol mwyach.

Yn ail, ac yn bwysicaf oll, rhaid inni sefydlu fframwaith cenedlaethol cynhwysfawr ar gyfer profi ac asesu tir a allai fod wedi'i halogi, gan flaenoriaethu'r safleoedd lle mae'r risg fwyaf, fel yr ardaloedd rwyf newydd sôn amdanynt nawr, yn enwedig pan fyddant yn trwytholchi i'n dyfrffyrdd, a darparu cefnogaeth ddiriaethol go iawn i'n hawdurdodau lleol fel y gallant gyflawni eu cyfrifoldebau statudol o'r diwedd. Ni allwn adael i gynghorau lleol, ein cymunedau, a'n trethdalwyr yn bwysicach fyth, i wynebu costau a pheryglon i iechyd yn sgil llygredd na wnaethant ei achosi—
